questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Carrying Capacity of a Logistic Growth Model
questions.problem:
Given that $y=y(t),$ what is the carrying capacity of the following logistic growth model?

$$
{y}^{′}=720y-8{y}^{2},\,y(0)=5
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
{y}^{′}=ky(a-y),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>y$ is the carrying capacity.

A diagram showing a typical logistic growth curve is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14045108/assets/57f4b604c546daed4f1cb3895191fae0ccac33b5c17aac705f203f0a837c7e69.png)

First, let's factor the right-hand side of the given equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{′}=8y(90-y),\,y(0)=5.
$$

From here, we see that $a=90.$ Therefore, the carrying capacity is $90.$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Carrying Capacity of a Logistic Growth Model In Context
questions.problem:
The population $y(t)$ of mockingbirds in a forest follows the logistic growth model

$$
{y}^{′}=0.6y-0.0003{y}^{2},\,y(0)=250,
$$

where $t$ is the time, in months, since the observations began. According to this model, what is the maximum possible population of mockingbirds?
questions.worked_solution:
A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
{y}^{′}=ky(a-y),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>y$ is the carrying capacity. 

The carrying capacity $a$ represents the maximum possible population. A diagram showing a typical logistic growth curve is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14045108/assets/57f4b604c546daed4f1cb3895191fae0ccac33b5c17aac705f203f0a837c7e69.png)

First, let's rewrite the right-hand side of the given equation so that it matches the form above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =0.6y-0.0003{y}^{2} \\  & =0.0003y(2\,000-y)\end{aligned}
$$

From here, we see that $a=2\,000.$ Hence, the carrying capacity is $2\,000,$ and we conclude that the number of mockingbirds cannot exceed $2\,000.$

questions.problem:
The population $y(t)$ of sloths in a forest follows the logistic growth model

$$
{y}^{′}=0.3y(2-\frac{y}{300}),\,y(0)=135,
$$

where $t$ is the time, in years, since the observations began. According to this model, what is the maximum possible sloth population?
questions.worked_solution:
A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
{y}^{′}=ky(a-y),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>y$ is the carrying capacity. 

The carrying capacity $a$ represents the maximum possible population. A diagram showing a typical logistic growth curve is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14045108/assets/57f4b604c546daed4f1cb3895191fae0ccac33b5c17aac705f203f0a837c7e69.png)

First, let's rewrite the right-hand side of the given equation so that it matches the form above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =0.3y(2-\frac{y}{300}) \\  & =0.3y(\frac{600-y}{300}) \\  & =\frac{0.3y}{300}(600-y) \\  & =0.001y(600-y)\end{aligned}
$$

From here, we see that $a=600.$ Hence, the carrying capacity is $600,$ and we conclude that the number of sloths cannot exceed $600.$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Point of Fastest Increase of a Logistic Growth Model
questions.problem:
The population $P(t)$of rabbits in a particular forest follows the logistic growth model

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=4P-0.002{P}^{2},\,P(0)=100,
$$

where $t$ is the time, measured in years. For which value of $P$ is the rabbit population growing at the fastest possible rate?
questions.worked_solution:
A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
{P}^{′}=kP(a-P),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.

For a logistic growth model, the fastest rate of growth occurs when $P=\frac{1}{2}a.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14045108/assets/9d8f5340bba4d3c407e43f2bc64a4aa2ea986be89b8024baaa4e8ae65e96e5d5.png)

First, let's rewrite the right-hand side of the given equation so that it matches the form above:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dP}{dt} & =4P-0.002{P}^{2} \\  & =0.002P(2\,000-P)\end{aligned}
$$

From here, we see that $a=2\,000.$ Hence, the carrying capacity is $2\,000,$ and $P$ grows at its fastest possible rate when 

$$
P=\frac{1}{2}a=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\,000=1\,000.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following differential equation for the function $y = y(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
y' = 2y\left(60 - \frac{y}{3} \right), \qquad y(0) = 10
$$

What is $\displaystyle \lim_{t\to\infty}{y(t)}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
y' = ky(a-y),
$$

where $k > 0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a > y$ is the carrying capacity.

A diagram showing a typical logistic growth curve is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14045108/assets/57f4b604c546daed4f1cb3895191fae0ccac33b5c17aac705f203f0a837c7e69.png)

First, let's rewrite the right-hand side of the given equation so that it matches the form above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =2y(60-\frac{y}{3}) \\  & =2y(\frac{180-y}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2y}{3}(180-y)\end{aligned}
$$

From here, we see that $a = 180.$ Hence, the carrying capacity is $180.$

For a given logistic growth model, $y\to a$ as $t\to\infty.$ Therefore,

$$
\lim_{t\to\infty}{y(t)} = 180.
$$

$$
